name: EGCG
lead: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG, epigallocatechin-3-gallate) is the most abundant catechin in tea, an ester of epigallocatechin and gallic acid. It occurs at high levels in dried green tea leaves (about 7,380 mg per 100 g), white tea and, in smaller amounts, black tea, and is sold in concentrated form in many dietary supplements.[1]

In physique and fat-loss circles it is taken as a fat-burner or pre-workout ingredient, often alongside caffeine-based thermogenics and L-carnitine, and some forum users have speculated about effects on myostatin.[4][5][6][7] Wikipedia describes EGCG as heavily studied in basic research with various biological effects in the laboratory, while the human evidence for specific health claims is limited.[1]

Safety is a documented concern at high doses: the European Food Safety Authority stated in 2018 that a daily intake of 800 mg or more of EGCG from supplements could raise the risk of liver damage, and the US FDA issued warning letters to EGCG supplement makers between 2008 and 2017 over disease claims and quality control.[1][8]

paras: EGCG extracts are marketed for fat loss and metabolic support. T Nation posters suggest taking an EGCG extract before training, sometimes with a thermogenic fat-burner, or using it during structured diets such as the Velocity Diet, and a supplement maker's page lists it among products for cellular, cardiovascular and metabolic health.[4][5][6][9]

Laboratory and clinical interest covers cancer prevention, inflammation, neurodegeneration and skin conditions, among others. Reviews summarise catechin effects on health, cancer and inflammation, and trials have examined topical EGCG in vitiligo and green tea extract for preventing colorectal adenomas.[10][11][12][13][14]

A 2016 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT02147041) tested high-dose green tea extract providing 856.8 mg of EGCG daily in 102 women with central obesity, with outcomes including weight, lipid profile and obesity-related hormone peptides.[15] A 2016 review cited by Wikipedia found that daily doses of 107 to 856 mg over four to 14 weeks produced a small reduction in LDL cholesterol, whereas a 2011 EFSA analysis could not establish a cause-and-effect link between tea catechins and normal LDL levels.[1]

A 2018 randomized trial examined polyphenol supplementation and intramuscular apoptotic signalling after acute resistance exercise.[16] A 2022 randomized trial tested green tea extract for preventing colorectal adenomas, and a 2021 trial tested topical EGCG in vitiligo.[11][12] Registered trials cover esophageal cancer symptoms, radiotherapy-related esophagitis, colorectal cancer chemoprevention, Down syndrome cognition and foetal alcohol syndrome, among others; an insulin-response trial in obesity and hypertension was registered but withdrawn.[17][18][19][20]
No published trial of EGCG in healthy lifters has established an effect on myostatin or muscle mass.

Wikipedia reports that oral EGCG is poorly absorbed even at intakes equivalent to 8 to 16 cups of green tea, which can cause nausea or heartburn.[1] A 2018 review concluded that excessive intake may cause liver toxicity, and EFSA concluded in 2018 that 800 mg or more per day could increase the risk of liver damage; the same sources describe 338 mg per day as considered safe in capsule form and 704 mg per day as safe when consumed as tea.[1][8] A United States Pharmacopeia review also examined the hepatotoxicity of green tea extracts, and a 2018 review examined the safety of green tea and extract consumption in adults.[21][22]
A T Nation poster notes that tea-derived products can cause morning nausea on an empty stomach.[23]

After oral intake EGCG levels in blood peak within about 1.7 hours, with an absorbed plasma half-life of around 5 hours and most unchanged EGCG excreted in urine within about 8 hours. Methylated metabolites have longer half-lives and reach 8 to 25 times the plasma levels of unmetabolised EGCG.[1]

In laboratory work EGCG has been reported to inhibit NF-kappa-B-dependent inflammatory signalling, inhibit DNA methyltransferase in cancer cell lines, remodel amyloid and alpha-synuclein fibrils, scavenge radicals, and activate AMPK, among many other effects whose relevance to people taking oral supplements is uncertain given low absorption.[24][25][26][27][28]

Between 2008 and 2017 the FDA sent several warning letters to makers of EGCG supplements, mostly for promoting them as treating or preventing diseases, which classifies them as unapproved new drugs, and one for inadequate quality assurance and labelling.[1] EGCG is sold under many supplement brands, and a T Nation thread discusses discontinued products from a supplement maker.[29]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding forums EGCG is treated as a fat-burner and general-health supplement, and a 2007-2008 thread speculated about myostatin inhibition.[4][5][6][30]

claims.claim: EGCG is a fat burner best taken pre-workout
claims.believers: Posters recommend taking an EGCG extract before training and pairing it with thermogenic products.[6][9]
claims.experts: A randomized trial of 856.8 mg EGCG daily in women with central obesity examined weight, lipids and hormones, and the broader literature on green tea extracts is mixed.[15]

claims.claim: EGCG inhibits myostatin and could help build muscle
claims.believers: A 2007 thread cites a laboratory abstract on Smad3 and Smad7 signalling and asks whether EGCG acts as a natural myostatin inhibitor.[30]
claims.experts: The cited work was mechanistic; no human trial in lifters has demonstrated myostatin inhibition or muscle gain by oral EGCG.

claims.claim: More EGCG is better and supplements are safe
claims.believers: Supplement makers promote concentrated EGCG for broad health support.[9]
claims.experts: EFSA states intake of 800 mg/day or more may increase liver-damage risk, and the FDA has warned several makers over claims and quality control.[1][8]
